transcript.text: Our Dyson (one of the V ones, purple bits) keeps cutting out after about 5-10 seconds. Not every time - some days it does a whole room fine. It's maybe 5 years old. Already cleaned the filter and checked for blockages. Battery or something else?

On a cordless Dyson like yours, cutting out after 5–10 seconds is rarely a random fault. It is almost always the machine protecting itself from either a blockage (which you’ve checked) or a battery issue. The most likely causes are:
1. Battery protection: The battery cells may be worn (common at 5 years old), causing the voltage to drop instantly under load, triggering a safety cut-out. Or, the machine is in 'Boost' mode which drains the battery very quickly.
2. Residual airflow restriction: Even if you cleared visible blockages, a filter that wasn't 100% dry or a small debris item stuck deeper in the cyclone can cause the motor to overheat and trip the thermal cut-out almost immediately. To narrow this down:
1. Was it set to Boost/Max mode when it happened? (This mode drains batteries rapidly and is normal behaviour for short bursts, but shouldn't kill a healthy battery in 5 seconds).
2. Does an LED light flash on the handle or bin when it cuts out? If so, which colour/pattern? Please check these two things.

Yes, on Max it nearly always stops within a few seconds, and it's less often on normal mode. When it cuts out the blue lights sometimes flash a few times, other times nothing at all. No red lights, and the battery isn't swollen or hot.

The fact that it cuts out almost instantly on Max mode but sometimes lasts longer on Normal, combined with the machine being 5 years old, points to the battery cells wearing out. Under the high power demand of Max mode, a worn battery’s voltage drops below the safety threshold immediately, triggering the cut-out you see as flashing blue lights (or no light if the system shuts down completely). However, we need to rule out a persistent airflow restriction or a damp filter tripping the thermal cut-out. Please charge it fully and test it on Normal mode only. If it runs normally on Normal but still cuts out instantly on Max, the battery is most likely worn and needs replacement. If it still cuts out quickly even on Normal after a full charge, there may be a blockage or damp filter we haven't cleared yet.

I haven't done that exact test yet. It's usually fine straight off the charger and worse once the battery's partly used, so a fresh-charge test might not tell us much. Can you say whether that pattern points to the battery? I'd like a straight answer on whether a £60+ battery is worth buying.

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
To answer your questions directly: Yes, that pattern points strongly to the battery. The fact that it runs fine straight off the charger (when voltage is highest) but cuts out after a few seconds once partly used (when voltage sags under load) is classic behaviour for worn lithium cells in a 5-year-old cordless vacuum. Max mode demands high current, which a degraded battery cannot sustain, triggering the safety cut-out. Regarding whether a £60+ battery is worth buying: it depends on your model's exact identity and availability. Dyson rarely publishes official spare part prices for older 'V' series models (like the V10/V11 variants often referred to as 'V ones'), and third-party batteries vary in quality. However, if official parts are unavailable or prohibitively expensive, replacement may not be economical. Since we cannot confirm the exact model number from 'V ONES' and Dyson's support for older cordless models has been limited, I recommend checking the base of your motor bar (where it connects to the handle) for a specific model code (e.g., V10, V11, etc.). If you find that code, you can check third-party retailers for compatible batteries. If no clear code exists or parts are unavailable, calling a specialist repair service or considering replacement is the next step.
I've checked the label and it says SV11. Does that help you say whether a £60+ battery is worth it?

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
Yes, knowing it is an SV11 (Dyson V10) helps. At 5 years old, the lithium-ion cells in the original battery are probably worn out. When you switch to Max mode, the current demand spikes, the voltage drops below the safety threshold instantly, and the machine shuts down to protect the battery. Regarding whether a £60+ battery is worth it: for a 5-year-old Dyson V10, I would advise against spending that much on a third-party battery. Third-party batteries vary wildly in quality and longevity; many will fail within a year or two. Given the age of the machine, replacing just the battery is rarely economically sensible unless you have a specific need for that exact model. 1. Accept the reduced runtime on Normal mode (if it still runs for 15-20 minutes) and use Max sparingly or not at all until you replace the unit.
2. Replace the entire vacuum cleaner with a newer model, which will give you better suction, longer battery life, and modern features. There is no owner-safe repair for this; the cells inside the battery pack are sealed and cannot be replaced individually without specialist equipment.

candidates: Battery protection or worn battery cells (high)
Thermal cut-out tripping due to residual blockage or damp filter (medium)
